Each wheel has 24 hues and eight rings from C = 0 to 0.25. Gaps are colors removed by the separation filter. The innermost ring repeats one gray at every hue, just as in the reference; the palette stores it only once if retained. A white dot marks an out-of-gamut target when enabled.

The 187 borrowed colors

Every swatch below comes unchanged from OKHSV Sketch. Black is fixed first; the other 186 fill the largest available perceptual gaps after the grid is filtered.

Sampling, selection, and gamut handling

The screenshots specify L = 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70, 0.85, 1.00; h = 0°, 15°, …, 345°; and C = j × 0.25/7 for j = 0…7. That is 1,344 positions, with 1,133 unique RGB results after clipping and rounding.

Selection fixes black and white, then repeatedly chooses the most distant eligible grid color until no remaining grid candidate meets ΔE00 ≥ 2. It then fills from the previous OKHSV palette under the same hard threshold. Source preference never overrides separation. This is a deterministic heuristic, not a proof of an optimal subset.

The wheels show requested Oklab coordinates, not constant-lightness slices of the final sRGB palette. Of the 1,344 targets, 763 lie outside sRGB. Independent channel clipping reproduces the supplied readouts, including Oklab (0.85, 0.25, 0) → RGB (255, 118, 199). It also changes lightness and hue: colorful results on the L = 1 wheel are no longer actually at L = 1. The inspector reports both requested and actual values.

This preserves the screenshot experiment. It does not claim that channel clipping is a perceptually neutral conversion; Ottosson explains the tradeoffs and alternatives. The JSON retains every target, clipping flag, selected status, and final coordinate.
